memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'"He shall remove all the fat from the bull of the sin offering—the fat that covers the internal organs or is connected to them, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the long lobe of the liver, which he will remove with the kidneys—just as the fat is removed from the ox sacrificed as a fellowship offering. Then the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering."'" - Lev 4:8-10 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Even in a sin offering — an offering occasioned by failure — the best parts still go up to God on the altar.

That is easy to miss, but it is quietly wonderful. The occasion is shameful. Someone has sinned. And yet God still receives the choicest portion, treated exactly as it was in the fellowship offering, the offering of celebration.

Sin does not cancel worship. It reshapes it.

Many believers withdraw from God after failing. They stop praying, stop reading, stop coming to church, waiting until they feel worthy enough to return. But Leviticus 4 has the sinner walking straight toward the altar, not away from it. The remedy for sin was found in God's presence, not at a distance from it.

David, after his worst failure, did not run. He wrote Psalm 51 — and in it he says, "My sacrifice, O God, is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart you, God, will not despise" (Ps 51:17).

If you have failed this week, do not wait until you feel clean to come to God. That is precisely backwards. Come because you are not clean. The altar was built for exactly this.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I withdraw from God when I fail, or run toward Him?
2. What am I waiting to "fix" before I feel able to approach God?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, I have hidden from You when I most needed to come. Thank You that Your altar was made for people like me. I come now, as I am. Amen.
